metadata.title: Rotation Numbers of Elements in Thompson's Group ${\bf T}$

nodes.name: Thompson's group ${\bf T}$ (dyadic circle homeomorphisms)
nodes.statement: One of these $\TT$, which will be the subject of this article, is the group of `dyadic' circle homeomorphisms $f:\S^1\to \S^1$. That is, if one takes $\S^1$ to be the interval $[0,1]$ with endpoints identified, then \begin{itemize} \item $f$ preserves the set of dyadic rational numbers (i.e., numbers of the form $p\cdot2^q$, $p,q\in\Z$), \item $f$ is linear except at a finite number of dyadic rational points, \item on each interval such that $f$ is linear, the derivative (i.e., slope) is a power of $2$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Thompson's group ${\bf T}$ is the group of circle homeomorphisms that are dyadic-rational preserving and piecewise linear with power-of-2 slopes.
differentia: $f$ preserves the set of dyadic rational numbers (i.e., numbers of the form $p\cdot2^q$, $p,q\in\Z$)
$f$ is linear except at a finite number of dyadic rational points
on each interval such that $f$ is linear, the derivative (i.e., slope) is a power of $2$

nodes.name: rotation number $\rho(f)$
nodes.statement: The \emph{rotation number} \cite{KH} of an orientation preserving circle homeomorphism $f:\S^1\to \S^1$ is the quantity \[ \rho(f)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\widetilde{f}^n(x)}{n} \mod \Z, \] where $\widetilde{f}:\R\to\R$ is any lift of $f$ to the universal cover $\R$, and $x\in\R$ is any initial point. Modulo $\Z$, the limit does not depend on the choices of $\widetilde{f}$ and $x$, and it is an important dynamical invariant for $f$.
nodes.statement_short: The rotation number is the mod-$\Z$ limit of $\widetilde{f}^n(x)/n$ for any lift and any starting point.
differentia: \[ \rho(f)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\widetilde{f}^n(x)}{n} \mod \Z, \]
of an orientation preserving circle homeomorphism $f:\S^1\to \S^1$
where $\widetilde{f}:\R\to\R$ is any lift of $f$ to the universal cover $\R$, and $x\in\R$ is any initial point

nodes.name: Rationality of $\rho(f)$ is equivalent to existence of a periodic point
nodes.statement: In particular $\rho(f)$ is rational if and only if $f$ has a periodic point.
conclusions: $\rho(f)$ is rational if and only if $f$ has a periodic point

nodes.name: Theorem A (Ghys-Sergiescu)
nodes.statement: \begin{itemize} \item[I.] For every element $f$ in Thompson's group ${\bf T}$, the rotation number $\rho(f)$ is rational. \item[II.] For every rational number $r$, there is an element $f\in{\bf T}$ such that $\rho(f)=r\mod\Z$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Rotation numbers of elements of Thompson's group ${\bf T}$ are exactly the rationals.
assumptions: For every element $f$ in Thompson's group ${\bf T}$
conclusions: there is an element $f\in{\bf T}$ such that $\rho(f)=r\mod\Z$

nodes.name: ray, generator, real ray
nodes.statement: Let $\R_+:=\{x\in\R\,|\,x\ge 0\}$ denote the set of non-negative real numbers. A {\em ray} in $\R^2$ is a rational one dimensional cone, i.e. a set of the form $\tau=\R_+ v$ for some $v\in\Z^2\setminus\{\origin\}$. The first lattice point $v\in\tau\cap(\Z^2\setminus\{\origin\})$ is called the \emph{generator} of $\tau$. We will call one dimensional cones with (possibly) irrational slope \emph{real rays}.
nodes.statement_short: A ray is a rational $1$-dimensional cone $\R_+ v$ with $v\in\Z^2$; its generator is its first lattice point, and cones of possibly irrational slope are real rays.
differentia: a set of the form $\tau=\R_+ v$ for some $v\in\Z^2\setminus\{\origin\}$

nodes.name: sector, facets, regular sector
nodes.statement: A {\em sector} is a rational two dimensional cone, i.e. a convex set $\sigma = \R_+ v_1 + \R_+ v_2$ for some $v_1,v_2\in\Z^2\setminus\{\origin\}$ linearly independent over $\R$. The rays $\tau_i = \R_+ v_i$, $i=1,2$, bounding $\sigma$ are called {\em facets} of $\sigma$. The sector $\sigma$ is \emph{regular} if the generators $v_1,v_2$ of the facets of $\sigma$ form a basis for $\Z^2$, i.e. if $|\det[v_1\ v_2]|= 1$.
nodes.statement_short: A sector is a rational $2$-dimensional cone spanned by two independent lattice vectors; it is regular when those generators have determinant $\pm1$.
differentia: a convex set $\sigma = \R_+ v_1 + \R_+ v_2$ for some $v_1,v_2\in\Z^2\setminus\{\origin\}$ linearly independent over $\R$

nodes.name: fan, support, complete fan, regular fan
nodes.statement: A \emph{fan} $\fan$ is a set of cones consisting of the zero-dimensional cone $\{\origin\}$, a finite sequence of rays $\tau_0,\tau_1,\cdots,\tau_d$ given in counterclockwise order, and the intervening sectors $\sigma_j$ bounded by $\tau_{j-1}$ and $\tau_j$, $1\leq j\leq d$. The support of $\fan$, denoted $\supp(\fan)$, is the union of all cones in $\fan$. We assume throughout that our fans are \emph{complete}, i.e. i.e., the sectors $\sigma_j$ in $\Delta$ cover $\R^2$ (hence $\tau_0 = \tau_d$). A fan is {\em regular} if all its sectors are regular.
nodes.statement_short: A fan is the origin together with a counterclockwise sequence of rays and the sectors between them; it is complete when the sectors cover $\R^2$ and regular when all sectors are regular.
differentia: consisting of the zero-dimensional cone $\{\origin\}$, a finite sequence of rays $\tau_0,\tau_1,\cdots,\tau_d$ given in counterclockwise order, and the intervening sectors $\sigma_j$ bounded by $\tau_{j-1}$ and $\tau_j$, $1\leq j\leq d$

nodes.name: piecewise linear map, fan compatible with $F$
nodes.statement: A continuous map $F:\R^2\to\R^2$ is {\em piecewise linear} if there exists a fan $\fan$ with sectors $\sigma_1,\cdots,\sigma_d$ and linear transformations $L_i:\R^2\to\R^2$, $i=1,\cdots,d$ such that $F|_{\sigma_i}=L_i|_{\sigma_i}$ for all $i=1,\cdots,d$. Any fan satisfying the above condition is said to be {\em compatible} with $F$. The map $F$ is orientation preserving if and only if each of $L_i$ is.
nodes.statement_short: $F$ is piecewise linear when it agrees with a linear map on each sector of some fan, and such a fan is called compatible with $F$.
differentia: there exists a fan $\fan$ with sectors $\sigma_1,\cdots,\sigma_d$ and linear transformations $L_i:\R^2\to\R^2$, $i=1,\cdots,d$ such that $F|_{\sigma_i}=L_i|_{\sigma_i}$ for all $i=1,\cdots,d$

nodes.name: piecewise linear automorphism of $\Z^2$
nodes.statement: A {\em piecewise linear automorphism of $\Z^2$} is an orientation preserving, piecewise linear homeomorphism $F:\R^2\to\R^2$ such that $F(\Z^2)=\Z^2$.
nodes.genus: an orientation preserving, piecewise linear homeomorphism $F:\R^2\to\R^2$

nodes.name: Linear pieces of a piecewise linear automorphism lie in $\SL(2,\Z)$
nodes.statement: If $F$ is a piecewise linear automorphism, then all the maps $L_i$ in the definition must have $\det(L_i)=1$, i.e., $L_i\in \SL(2,\Z)$. It follows that if $\Delta$ is a regular fan compatible with $F$, then the fan $F(\Delta)$ obtained by mapping forward all cones in $\Delta$ is also regular, though it is not necessarily compatible with $F$.
nodes.statement_short: The linear pieces of a piecewise linear automorphism are unimodular, so images of regular fans stay regular (but need not stay compatible).
assumptions: $\Delta$ is a regular fan compatible with $F$
conclusions: all the maps $L_i$ in the definition must have $\det(L_i)=1$, i.e., $L_i\in \SL(2,\Z)$
the fan $F(\Delta)$ obtained by mapping forward all cones in $\Delta$ is also regular, though it is not necessarily compatible with $F$

nodes.name: standard dyadic sub-interval
nodes.statement: A dyadic sub-interval $I\subset[0,1]$ is called {\em standard} if it is of the form $I = [\frac{a}{2^k},\frac{a+1}{2^k}]$. For example, the interval $[\frac 1 4,\frac 1 2]$ is dyadic and standard, whereas $[\frac 1 4,\frac 3 4]$ is dyadic but not standard.
differentia: it is of the form $I = [\frac{a}{2^k},\frac{a+1}{2^k}]$

nodes.name: Standard versus non-standard dyadic intervals
nodes.statement: For example, the interval $[\frac 1 4,\frac 1 2]$ is dyadic and standard, whereas $[\frac 1 4,\frac 3 4]$ is dyadic but not standard.

nodes.name: local homeomorphism $\phi:\RR_\sigma\to I$ (Stern-Brocot averaging)
nodes.statement: This is accomplished locally as follows. Let $I = [\frac{a}{2^k},\frac{a+1}{2^k}]$ be a ``dyadic standard\footnote{A dyadic sub-interval $I\subset[0,1]$ is called {\em standard} if it is of the form $I = [\frac{a}{2^k},\frac{a+1}{2^k}]$. For example, the interval $[\frac 1 4,\frac 1 2]$ is dyadic and standard, whereas $[\frac 1 4,\frac 3 4]$ is dyadic but not standard. }'' interval and $\sigma\subset \R^2$ be a regular sector generated by the (oriented) basis $v_1,v_2\subset \Z^2$. Taking $\RR_\sigma\subset \RR$ to be the set of real rays in $\sigma$, we define a homeomorphism $\phi:\RR_\sigma\to I$ as follows, identifying each rational ray with its generator $v\in\Z^2$. We first assign facets to endpoints: $\phi(v_1) = \frac{a}{2^k}$ and $\phi(v_2) = \frac{a+1}{2^k}$. Then we proceed inductively by averaging: $\phi(v_1+v_2) = \frac12(\phi(v_1) + \phi(v_2))$, and more generally, if $\phi$ is defined at two primitive points (i.e. integral points where the two coordinates are coprime) $v,v'\in\sigma\cap \Z^2$ but at no points in the intervening sector, then we set $\phi(v+v') = \frac12(\phi(v)+\phi(v'))$. One checks that this procedure results in an order-preserving bijection between rational rays in $\sigma$ and dyadic points in $I$ which therefore extends to an orientation-preserving homeomorphism $\phi:\RR_\sigma \to I$.
nodes.statement_short: $\phi$ sends the two facet generators of a regular sector to the endpoints of a standard dyadic interval and extends by mediant-to-midpoint averaging to an order-preserving homeomorphism.
differentia: We first assign facets to endpoints: $\phi(v_1) = \frac{a}{2^k}$ and $\phi(v_2) = \frac{a+1}{2^k}$
Then we proceed inductively by averaging: $\phi(v_1+v_2) = \frac12(\phi(v_1) + \phi(v_2))$

nodes.name: Minkowski's question mark function
nodes.statement: Note that when $I=[0,1]$ and $\sigma$ is the cone generated by $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)\in\R^2$ with $\RR_\sigma$ parameterized by the slope, $\phi$ is known as \emph{Minkowski's question mark function}.

nodes.name: globalization of $\phi$
nodes.statement: One globalizes $\phi$ by choosing any partition $\R^2 = \sigma_1\cup\dots\cup\sigma_d$ into regular sectors and a corresponding partition $[0,1]=I_1\cup\dots\cup I_d$ into standard dyadic intervals and defining $\phi|_{\RR_{\sigma_j}}:\RR_{\sigma_j}\to I_j$ sector-wise as above.

nodes.name: Local conjugation identity $\phi'\circ F = f\circ \phi$
nodes.statement: To see that $\phi$ conjugates piecewise linear automorphisms of $\Z^2$ to dyadic circle maps, it suffices to verify the following additional fact. Let $\phi:\RR_\sigma \to I$ be the `local' version of $\phi$ defined above. Let $\sigma'$ be another regular sector, $I'$ another standard dyadic interval, and $\phi':\RR_{\sigma'}\to I'$ the analogous homeomorphism. Then $\phi'\circ F = f\circ \phi$ where $F\in \SL(2,\Z)$ is the unique element such that $F(\sigma) = \sigma'$ and $f:\R\to\R$ is the unique increasing affine map such that $f(I) = I'$.
nodes.statement_short: The local charts $\phi$ intertwine the unimodular map taking one regular sector to another with the affine map taking one standard dyadic interval to another.
assumptions: Let $\phi:\RR_\sigma \to I$ be the `local' version of $\phi$ defined above
Let $\sigma'$ be another regular sector, $I'$ another standard dyadic interval, and $\phi':\RR_{\sigma'}\to I'$ the analogous homeomorphism
$F\in \SL(2,\Z)$ is the unique element such that $F(\sigma) = \sigma'$
$f:\R\to\R$ is the unique increasing affine map such that $f(I) = I'$

nodes.name: refinement of a fan
nodes.statement: A \emph{refinement} of a fan $\Delta$ is a fan $\Delta'$ with the same support as $\Delta$ and such that for every cone $\sigma'\in\fan'$, there exists $\sigma\in\fan$ such that $\sigma'\subseteq\sigma$.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\Z^2$
nodes.genus: a fan $\Delta'$ with the same support as $\Delta$
differentia: for every cone $\sigma'\in\fan'$, there exists $\sigma\in\fan$ such that $\sigma'\subseteq\sigma$

nodes.name: Lemma 3.1 (existence of a regular refinement)
nodes.statement: Any fan admits a regular refinement.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\Z^2$
nodes.origin_citation: well-known in convex geometry (no specific reference given by the authors)
conclusions: Any fan admits a regular refinement.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement: It suffices to prove that any sector $\sigma$ may be partitioned into regular sectors. If $\sigma$ is not regular, then the ray generators $u_1,u_2$ of its facets must satisfy $|\det[u_1\ u_2]|\ge 2$. This implies that there must be at least one primitive point $w$ in the interior of the parallelogram formed by $u_1$ and $u_2$. The ray $\R_+ w$ divides $\sigma$ into two new sectors. Since $|\det[w\ u_i]| < |\det[u_1\ u_2]|$, $i=1,2$, we see that finitely many such subdivisions will result in a partition of $\sigma$ into regular sectors.
nodes.statement_short: Subdivide a non-regular sector along an interior primitive point; the determinant strictly drops, so finitely many subdivisions leave only regular sectors.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\Z^2$

nodes.name: Reduce to a single sector
nodes.statement: It suffices to prove that any sector $\sigma$ may be partitioned into regular sectors.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce the fan statement to partitioning one sector into regular sectors.

nodes.name: Split along an interior primitive point
nodes.statement: If $\sigma$ is not regular, then the ray generators $u_1,u_2$ of its facets must satisfy $|\det[u_1\ u_2]|\ge 2$. This implies that there must be at least one primitive point $w$ in the interior of the parallelogram formed by $u_1$ and $u_2$. The ray $\R_+ w$ divides $\sigma$ into two new sectors.
nodes.statement_short: A non-regular sector has determinant at least $2$, hence an interior primitive point $w$ whose ray splits it in two.

nodes.name: Termination by determinant descent
nodes.statement: Since $|\det[w\ u_i]| < |\det[u_1\ u_2]|$, $i=1,2$, we see that finitely many such subdivisions will result in a partition of $\sigma$ into regular sectors.
nodes.statement_short: The determinant strictly decreases at each split, so the process terminates in regular sectors.

nodes.name: simple split and simple merge of a fan
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma\in\fan$ be a regular sector with its boundary rays generated by $u_1,u_2\in\Z^2$. Let $\tau\subset \sigma$ be the ray generated by some point $u\in\Z^2$ in the interior of $\sigma$. Then $\sigma\setminus\tau$ is a union of two disjoint sectors $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$. One checks that they are both regular if and only if $u=u_1+u_2$. We then call the fan $\fan'=(\fan\setminus\{\sigma\})\cup\{\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\tau\}$ the {\em simple split} of $\fan$ at $\sigma$. If $\fan$ is regular then so is $\fan'$. Conversely, we call $\Delta$ the {\em simple merge} of $\Delta'$ at $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$.
nodes.statement_short: A simple split barycentrically subdivides a regular sector along the ray through $u_1+u_2$; the inverse operation is a simple merge.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\Z^2$
differentia: $\tau\subset \sigma$ be the ray generated by some point $u\in\Z^2$ in the interior of $\sigma$
they are both regular if and only if $u=u_1+u_2$

nodes.name: Lemma 3.2 (regular refinements come from simple splits)
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\fan,\fan'$ are regular fans, and $\fan'$ refines $\fan$. Then one can obtain $\fan'$ from $\fan$ by a sequence of simple splits.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\Z^2$
nodes.origin_citation: well-known in convex geometry (no specific reference given by the authors)
conclusions: one can obtain $\fan'$ from $\fan$ by a sequence of simple splits

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.2
nodes.statement: We need to consider only the case where $\fan$ is the fan determined by a single regular sector $\sigma := \R_+ u + \R_+ v$. Working inductively, it suffices to show that either $\fan'$ includes the ray $\tau := \R_+ (u+v)$ that barycentrically subdivies $\sigma$, or $\Delta' = \Delta$. If $\tau \notin \Delta'$, then we let $\tau_1 = \R_+(au + bv)$, $\tau_2 = \R_+(cu + dv)$ be the facets of the sector $\sigma' \in \Delta'$ that contains $\tau$. We may assume that $a > b\geq 0$ and $d> c\geq 0$ are all integers. Since $\sigma'$ is regular, we get $$ 1 = ad-bc \geq (b+1)(c+1) - bc = b+c+1. $$ Thus $b=c = 0$ and $a=d=1$, i.e. $\sigma' = \sigma$ and $\fan' = \fan$.
nodes.statement_short: Induct on the barycentric ray: if it is missing from $\Delta'$, unimodularity of the containing sector forces $b=c=0$, $a=d=1$, so $\Delta'=\Delta$.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\Z^2$

nodes.name: Reduce to a single regular sector
nodes.statement: We need to consider only the case where $\fan$ is the fan determined by a single regular sector $\sigma := \R_+ u + \R_+ v$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the fan of one regular sector.

nodes.name: Inductive reduction to the barycentric ray
nodes.statement: Working inductively, it suffices to show that either $\fan'$ includes the ray $\tau := \R_+ (u+v)$ that barycentrically subdivies $\sigma$, or $\Delta' = \Delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Set up the induction: show $\Delta'$ either contains the barycentric ray or equals $\Delta$.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\Z^2$

nodes.name: Suppose the barycentric ray is missing
nodes.statement: If $\tau \notin \Delta'$, then we let $\tau_1 = \R_+(au + bv)$, $\tau_2 = \R_+(cu + dv)$ be the facets of the sector $\sigma' \in \Delta'$ that contains $\tau$. We may assume that $a > b\geq 0$ and $d> c\geq 0$ are all integers.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $\tau\notin\Delta'$ and coordinatize the facets of the sector containing $\tau$.

nodes.name: Determinant inequality forces $\sigma'=\sigma$
nodes.statement: Since $\sigma'$ is regular, we get $$ 1 = ad-bc \geq (b+1)(c+1) - bc = b+c+1. $$ Thus $b=c = 0$ and $a=d=1$, i.e. $\sigma' = \sigma$ and $\fan' = \fan$.
nodes.statement_short: Unimodularity gives $1\ge b+c+1$, hence $b=c=0$, $a=d=1$, and $\Delta'=\Delta$.

nodes.name: isomorphism, simple split, simple merge, and simple map from $\Delta$ to $\Delta'$
nodes.statement: From now on, $F$ will always denote a piecewise linear automorphism of $\Z^2$. Our proof of Theorem A amounts to carefully analyzing how fans transform under $F$. Note that if $\Delta$ is a regular fan compatible with $F$, then the image fan $F(\Delta) :=\{F(\sigma):\sigma\in \Delta\}$ is also regular. If $\Delta'$ is another regular fan, then we say that $F$ is an {\em isomorphism} from $\Delta$ to $\Delta'$ if $F(\Delta) = \Delta'$. Similarly, we say that $F$ is a {\em simple split} or {\em simple merge} of $\fan'$ if $F(\Delta)$ is accordingly, a simple split or simple merge of $\Delta'$. We call $F$ a {\em simple} map from $\Delta$ to $\Delta'$ if $F$ is of one of these three types.
nodes.statement_short: $F$ is simple from $\Delta$ to $\Delta'$ when $F(\Delta)$ is $\Delta'$ itself, a simple split of it, or a simple merge of it.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\Z^2$
differentia: $F$ is of one of these three types

nodes.name: approximate map $F_\sharp:\Delta\to\Delta'$
nodes.statement: Regardless, we associate to $F$ a partially defined, `approximate' map $F_\sharp:\Delta\to\Delta'$ as follows: for each $\sigma\in\fan$, we take $F_\sharp\sigma$ to be the smallest cone in $\fan'$ containing $F(\sigma)$. If no single cone in $\fan'$ contains $F(\sigma)$, then we leave $F_\sharp\sigma$ undefined. Hence $F_\sharp\tau$ is defined for all rays $\tau\in\fan$, though the image might be a sector or a ray; whereas for each sector $\sigma\in\Delta$, the cone $F_\sharp \sigma$ is either another sector or undefined.
nodes.statement_short: $F_\sharp\sigma$ is the smallest cone of $\Delta'$ containing $F(\sigma)$, undefined when no such cone exists.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\Z^2$
differentia: for each $\sigma\in\fan$, we take $F_\sharp\sigma$ to be the smallest cone in $\fan'$ containing $F(\sigma)$
If no single cone in $\fan'$ contains $F(\sigma)$, then we leave $F_\sharp\sigma$ undefined

nodes.name: Functoriality of the approximate map
nodes.statement: If $G$ is another piecewise linear automorphism of $\Z^2$ and $G_\sharp:\fan'\to\fan''$ is an approximate map of fans, then we have $G_\sharp F_\sharp \sigma = (G\circ F)_\sharp\sigma$ provided that the left side is defined.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate maps compose functorially wherever the composite is defined.

assumptions: $G$ is another piecewise linear automorphism of $\Z^2$
$G_\sharp:\fan'\to\fan''$ is an approximate map of fans

nodes.name: Proposition 3.3 (decomposition into simple maps)
nodes.statement: Let $\fan$ be a regular fan compatible with $F$. Then there is a decomposition $F=f_{n-1}\circ\dots \circ f_0$ into piecewise linear automorphisms of $\Z^2$ and a corresponding sequence of regular fans $\Delta_0,\dots,\Delta_n$ such that \begin{itemize} \item $\Delta_0 = \Delta_n = \Delta$; \item $\Delta_j$ is compatible with $f_j$ for $0\leq j\leq n-1$; \item $f_j$ is a simple map from $\Delta_j$ to $\Delta_{j+1}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Every piecewise linear automorphism factors as a composition of simple maps through a cycle of regular fans returning to $\Delta$.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\Z^2$
assumptions: $\fan$ be a regular fan compatible with $F$
conclusions: there is a decomposition $F=f_{n-1}\circ\dots \circ f_0$ into piecewise linear automorphisms of $\Z^2$ and a corresponding sequence of regular fans $\Delta_0,\dots,\Delta_n$
$\Delta_j$ is compatible with $f_j$ for $0\leq j\leq n-1$
$f_j$ is a simple map from $\Delta_j$ to $\Delta_{j+1}$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.3
nodes.statement: First, set $f_0=F$ and $\fan_1=F(\fan)$. Lemma \ref{lem:regularization} then gives a regular common refinement $\fan'$ of $\fan$ and $F(\fan)$. Then by Lemma~\ref{lem:regular_refinement}, we know that we can obtain $\fan'$ from $F(\fan)$ by performing finitely many simple splits, i.e. we have a sequence \[ \xymatrix{ \fan \ar[rr]^{F} && \fan_1=F(\fan) \ar[rr]^{\id} && \fan_2 \ar[rr]^{\id} &&\cdots \ar[rr]^{\id} && \fan_k=\fan' } \] in which all but the first arrow represents a simple split; and the first arrow is an isomorphism. Similarly, there is a sequence \[ \xymatrix{ \fan_k=\fan' \ar[rr]^{\id} && \fan_{k+1} \ar[rr]^{\id} &&\cdots \ar[rr]^{\id} && \fan_{n-1} \ar[rr]^{\id} && \fan = \fan_n } \] such that each arrow is a simple merge, $i=k,\cdots,n-1$. Putting the two sequences together completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Split $F(\Delta)$ up to a common regular refinement, then merge back down to $\Delta$, and concatenate the two chains of simple maps.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\Z^2$

nodes.name: Initialize and take a common regular refinement
nodes.statement: First, set $f_0=F$ and $\fan_1=F(\fan)$. Lemma \ref{lem:regularization} then gives a regular common refinement $\fan'$ of $\fan$ and $F(\fan)$.
nodes.statement_short: Start with $f_0=F$ and use Lemma 3.1 to get a common regular refinement $\Delta'$.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\Z^2$

nodes.name: Chain of simple splits up to $\Delta'$
nodes.statement: Then by Lemma~\ref{lem:regular_refinement}, we know that we can obtain $\fan'$ from $F(\fan)$ by performing finitely many simple splits, i.e. we have a sequence \[ \xymatrix{ \fan \ar[rr]^{F} && \fan_1=F(\fan) \ar[rr]^{\id} && \fan_2 \ar[rr]^{\id} &&\cdots \ar[rr]^{\id} && \fan_k=\fan' } \] in which all but the first arrow represents a simple split; and the first arrow is an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 3.2 to write $F(\Delta)\to\Delta'$ as finitely many simple splits after the initial isomorphism.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\Z^2$

nodes.name: Chain of simple merges back to $\Delta$
nodes.statement: Similarly, there is a sequence \[ \xymatrix{ \fan_k=\fan' \ar[rr]^{\id} && \fan_{k+1} \ar[rr]^{\id} &&\cdots \ar[rr]^{\id} && \fan_{n-1} \ar[rr]^{\id} && \fan = \fan_n } \] such that each arrow is a simple merge, $i=k,\cdots,n-1$.
nodes.statement_short: Reverse the refinement from $\Delta'$ back to $\Delta$ by a chain of simple merges.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\Z^2$

nodes.name: Concatenate the two sequences
nodes.statement: Putting the two sequences together completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Concatenating the split chain and the merge chain yields the decomposition.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\Z^2$

nodes.name: deterministic cone
nodes.statement: We call a cone $\tau\in\Delta$ {\em deterministic} for the approximate self-map $F_\sharp:\Delta\to\Delta$ if all its approximate forward images $(F_\sharp)^j\tau$, $j\ge 1$, are defined.
differentia: all its approximate forward images $(F_\sharp)^j\tau$, $j\ge 1$, are defined

nodes.name: Proposition 4.1 (existence of a refinement with all rays deterministic)
nodes.statement: For any piecewise linear automorphism $F$ and any fan $\fan$, there exists a regular refinement $\fan'$ of $\fan$ such that $\fan'$ is regular and compatible with $F$, and every ray in $\fan'$ is deterministic for $F_\sharp:\Delta'\to\Delta'$.
nodes.statement_short: Any fan can be refined to a regular, $F$-compatible fan all of whose rays are deterministic for $F_\sharp$.
conclusions: there exists a regular refinement $\fan'$ of $\fan$ such that $\fan'$ is regular and compatible with $F$
every ray in $\fan'$ is deterministic for $F_\sharp:\Delta'\to\Delta'$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.1
nodes.statement:
Let $f_j$ and $\Delta_j$ be the maps and associated fans in the decomposition of $F$ from Proposition ef{prop:decomposition}. Since $\Delta_0 = \Delta_n$, we may extend these sequences of maps/fans periodically, e.g. $f_j := f_{j\mod n}$ for all $j\in\N$. Suppose that there exists a ray $	au\in\Delta$ that is not deterministic for $F_\sharp:\Delta	o\Delta$. In particular, we know $F(\Delta)
eq \Delta$, so $n\geq 2$. Then by replacing $	au$ with an approximate forward image, we may assume that $F_\sharp 	au = \sigma$ is a sector and that $(F_\sharp)^k \sigma$ is undefined for $k\in\N$ large enough. We may refine this observation using the decomposition of $F$. Namely, there exist indices $i < k \in\N$, and a ray $	au_i\in\Delta_i$ such that  egin{itemize} \item[(i)] $\sigma_{i+1} := f_{i\sharp} 	au_i \in \Delta_{i+1}$ is a sector; \item[(ii)] $\sigma_{j+1} := f_{j\sharp}\sigma_j \in  an_{j+1}$ is well-defined for $ j =i+1,\cdots, k-1$, but $f_{k\sharp}\sigma_{k}$ is not defined; \item[(iii)] $i,	au_i,k$ are chosen so that $k-i$ is as small as possible given the first two conditions. \end{itemize} That is, we attend to the following sequence: \[ \xymatrix{ 	au_i\in an_{i} \ar[rr]^{f_i} && \sigma_{i+1}\in an_{i+1} \ar[rr]^{f_{i+1}} &&\cdots \ar[rr]^{f_{k-1}} && \sigma_{k}\in an_k \ar[rr]^{f_k} &&  an_{k+1} } \] The idea is to inductively refine the fans $ an_{i+1},\cdots, an_{k}$ so that $f_k$ becomes an isomorphism. Condition (i) together with the fact that $f_i$ is simple from $\Delta_i$ to $\Delta_{i+1}$ means that $	au_{i+1} := f_i(	au_i)$ is the unique ray that divides $\sigma_{i+1}$ into two regular cones. Replacing $\sigma_{i+1}$ with these two cones and adding the ray $	au_{i+1}$ to $\Delta_{i+1}$ turns the map $f_i:\Delta_i	o\Delta_{i+1}$ into an isomorphism from $\Delta_i$ to $\Delta_{i+1}$. Note that in this (and succeeding) steps, we apply the same refinement to all fans $\Delta_{i+\ell n}$ equivalent mod $n$ to $\Delta_i$. Since $n\geq 2$ this does not affect the outcome. Turning from $f_i$ to $f_{i+1}$, we find two possible cases. If $i+1=k$, then $f_{i+1}(\sigma_{i+1})$ is equal to the union of two adjacent sectors in $\Delta_{i+2}$. Since the above refinement of $\Delta_{i+1}$ split $\sigma_{i+1}$ into two regular cones, $f_{i+1}$ is now an isomorphism from $\Delta_{i+1}$ to $\Delta_{i+2}$. Otherwise, $i+1<k$. If $f_{i+1}$ was initially a merge, then there is another ray $	ilde	au_{i+1}\in\Delta_{i+1}$ such that $f_{i+1}(	ilde	au_{i+1})
otin\Delta_{i+2}$. However, our minimality assumption on $k-i$ guarantees that the images $f_{i+1}(	ilde	au_{i+1})$ and $f_{i+1}(	au_{i+1})$ lie in different sectors. Hence regardless of whether $f_{i+1}$ is a merge or not, $f_{i+1}(	au_{i+1})$ divides $\sigma_{i+2}$ into two \emph{regular} cones. So as with $\Delta_{i+1}$, we can refine $\Delta_{i+2}$ by splitting $\sigma_{i+2}$ into two regular sectors, the result being that $f_{i+1}$ remains a simple map. In this case, we move on to $f_{i+2}$ and repeat the process until we reach $f_k$. In the end, $f_k$ is improved from a split to an isomorphism, and maps $f_j$ with $j
ot\equiv k\mod n$ remain simple of the same type as before. If there remain rays in $\Delta=\Delta_0$ that are not deterministic for $F_\sharp$, then we repeat the process. Since there are only finitely many $f_j$ (modulo $n$), finitely many repetitions leads to a situation in which either all rays in $\Delta$ are deterministic or all $f_j$ are isomorphisms. In the latter case $F$ is itself an isomorphism from $\Delta$ to $\Delta$, and all rays are deterministic anyhow.
nodes.statement_short: Take a minimal-length bad sequence in the simple-map decomposition and inductively refine the intermediate fans until the failing map becomes an isomorphism; finitely many repetitions make every ray deterministic.

nodes.name: Periodically extend the decomposition
nodes.statement: Let $f_j$ and $\Delta_j$ be the maps and associated fans in the decomposition of $F$ from Proposition \ref{prop:decomposition}. Since $\Delta_0 = \Delta_n$, we may extend these sequences of maps/fans periodically, e.g. $f_j := f_{j\mod n}$ for all $j\in\N$.
nodes.statement_short: Invoke Proposition 3.3 and extend the resulting maps and fans periodically in $j$.

nodes.name: Assume a non-deterministic ray exists
nodes.statement: Suppose that there exists a ray $\tau\in\Delta$ that is not deterministic for $F_\sharp:\Delta\to\Delta$. In particular, we know $F(\Delta)\neq \Delta$, so $n\geq 2$. Then by replacing $\tau$ with an approximate forward image, we may assume that $F_\sharp \tau = \sigma$ is a sector and that $(F_\sharp)^k \sigma$ is undefined for $k\in\N$ large enough.
nodes.statement_short: Assume some ray is not deterministic and normalize it so its image is a sector whose forward orbit eventually fails.

nodes.name: Choose a minimal failing window $i<k$
nodes.statement: We may refine this observation using the decomposition of $F$. Namely, there exist indices $i < k \in\N$, and a ray $\tau_i\in\Delta_i$ such that \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $\sigma_{i+1} := f_{i\sharp} \tau_i \in \Delta_{i+1}$ is a sector; \item[(ii)] $\sigma_{j+1} := f_{j\sharp}\sigma_j \in \fan_{j+1}$ is well-defined for $ j =i+1,\cdots, k-1$, but $f_{k\sharp}\sigma_{k}$ is not defined; \item[(iii)] $i,\tau_i,k$ are chosen so that $k-i$ is as small as possible given the first two conditions. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Extract indices $i<k$ and a ray $\tau_i$ with a minimal window over which the approximate images stay defined but then fail.

nodes.name: State the refinement strategy
nodes.statement: That is, we attend to the following sequence: \[ \xymatrix{ \tau_i\in\fan_{i} \ar[rr]^{f_i} && \sigma_{i+1}\in\fan_{i+1} \ar[rr]^{f_{i+1}} &&\cdots \ar[rr]^{f_{k-1}} && \sigma_{k}\in\fan_k \ar[rr]^{f_k} && \fan_{k+1} } \] The idea is to inductively refine the fans $\fan_{i+1},\cdots,\fan_{k}$ so that $f_k$ becomes an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Display the failing chain and announce the plan: refine $\Delta_{i+1},\dots,\Delta_k$ so $f_k$ becomes an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Refine $\Delta_{i+1}$ to make $f_i$ an isomorphism
nodes.statement: Condition (i) together with the fact that $f_i$ is simple from $\Delta_i$ to $\Delta_{i+1}$ means that $\tau_{i+1} := f_i(\tau_i)$ is the unique ray that divides $\sigma_{i+1}$ into two regular cones. Replacing $\sigma_{i+1}$ with these two cones and adding the ray $\tau_{i+1}$ to $\Delta_{i+1}$ turns the map $f_i:\Delta_i\to\Delta_{i+1}$ into an isomorphism from $\Delta_i$ to $\Delta_{i+1}$. Note that in this (and succeeding) steps, we apply the same refinement to all fans $\Delta_{i+\ell n}$ equivalent mod $n$ to $\Delta_i$. Since $n\geq 2$ this does not affect the outcome.
nodes.statement_short: Add the ray $f_i(\tau_i)$ to $\Delta_{i+1}$ (and its mod-$n$ copies), upgrading $f_i$ to an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Case $i+1=k$
nodes.statement: Turning from $f_i$ to $f_{i+1}$, we find two possible cases. If $i+1=k$, then $f_{i+1}(\sigma_{i+1})$ is equal to the union of two adjacent sectors in $\Delta_{i+2}$. Since the above refinement of $\Delta_{i+1}$ split $\sigma_{i+1}$ into two regular cones, $f_{i+1}$ is now an isomorphism from $\Delta_{i+1}$ to $\Delta_{i+2}$.
nodes.statement_short: When the window has length one, the refinement already makes $f_{i+1}$ an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Case $i+1<k$ and propagation to $f_k$
nodes.statement: Otherwise, $i+1<k$. If $f_{i+1}$ was initially a merge, then there is another ray $\tilde\tau_{i+1}\in\Delta_{i+1}$ such that $f_{i+1}(\tilde\tau_{i+1})\notin\Delta_{i+2}$. However, our minimality assumption on $k-i$ guarantees that the images $f_{i+1}(\tilde\tau_{i+1})$ and $f_{i+1}(\tau_{i+1})$ lie in different sectors. Hence regardless of whether $f_{i+1}$ is a merge or not, $f_{i+1}(\tau_{i+1})$ divides $\sigma_{i+2}$ into two \emph{regular} cones. So as with $\Delta_{i+1}$, we can refine $\Delta_{i+2}$ by splitting $\sigma_{i+2}$ into two regular sectors, the result being that $f_{i+1}$ remains a simple map. In this case, we move on to $f_{i+2}$ and repeat the process until we reach $f_k$. In the end, $f_k$ is improved from a split to an isomorphism, and maps $f_j$ with $j\not\equiv k\mod n$ remain simple of the same type as before.
nodes.statement_short: Minimality of $k-i$ lets the refinement propagate step by step until $f_k$ is upgraded from a split to an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Iterate finitely often to finish
nodes.statement: If there remain rays in $\Delta=\Delta_0$ that are not deterministic for $F_\sharp$, then we repeat the process. Since there are only finitely many $f_j$ (modulo $n$), finitely many repetitions leads to a situation in which either all rays in $\Delta$ are deterministic or all $f_j$ are isomorphisms. In the latter case $F$ is itself an isomorphism from $\Delta$ to $\Delta$, and all rays are deterministic anyhow.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat finitely many times; either all rays become deterministic or $F$ becomes an isomorphism, which also makes them deterministic.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem A, part I
nodes.statement: Given any piecewise linear automorphism $F$ of $\Z^2$, we first find any fan $\fan$ such that $\fan$ is compatible with $F$. Next, we find a regular refinement $\fan'$ of $\fan$, then $\fan'$ is still compatible with $F$. Finally, we find a further refinement $\fan''$ such that every ray in $\fan''$ is deterministic for $F_\sharp$. Observe how $F$ acts on the rays and sectors of $\fan''$, either one of the following will happen: \begin{itemize} \item There is never a ray mapped into a sector, so rays always map to rays, and $F$ is permuting the rays. In this case, some iterate of every ray is going back to itself and $F$ is of finite order. \item There is a ray maps into a sector $\sigma$, then $\sigma$ must be deterministic for $F_\sharp$, and $(F_\sharp)^j \sigma$, $j\ge 1$, are all defined and are sectors. Then again, we have finitely many sectors, there must be some $i<j$ such that $(F_\sharp)^i \sigma=(F_\sharp)^j \sigma$. As a consequence, there is a ray in $(F_\sharp)^i \sigma$ that is fixed by $F^{j-i}$, so the circle map induced by $F$ has a periodic point. \end{itemize} In either case, the rotation number of $F$ is rational because there is a periodic point. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Refine to a fan whose rays are all deterministic; a pigeonhole on the finitely many sectors produces a periodic ray, hence a periodic point and a rational rotation number.

nodes.name: Find a compatible fan
nodes.statement: Given any piecewise linear automorphism $F$ of $\Z^2$, we first find any fan $\fan$ such that $\fan$ is compatible with $F$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick any fan compatible with $F$.

nodes.name: Pass to a regular refinement
nodes.statement: Next, we find a regular refinement $\fan'$ of $\fan$, then $\fan'$ is still compatible with $F$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 3.1 to get a regular refinement that is still compatible with $F$.

nodes.name: Refine so that every ray is deterministic
nodes.statement: Finally, we find a further refinement $\fan''$ such that every ray in $\fan''$ is deterministic for $F_\sharp$. Observe how $F$ acts on the rays and sectors of $\fan''$, either one of the following will happen:
nodes.statement_short: Apply Proposition 4.1 to make every ray deterministic, then split into two cases.

nodes.name: Case: $F$ permutes the rays
nodes.statement: There is never a ray mapped into a sector, so rays always map to rays, and $F$ is permuting the rays. In this case, some iterate of every ray is going back to itself and $F$ is of finite order.
nodes.statement_short: If rays always map to rays, $F$ permutes finitely many rays and has finite order.

nodes.name: Case: some ray maps into a sector
nodes.statement: There is a ray maps into a sector $\sigma$, then $\sigma$ must be deterministic for $F_\sharp$, and $(F_\sharp)^j \sigma$, $j\ge 1$, are all defined and are sectors. Then again, we have finitely many sectors, there must be some $i<j$ such that $(F_\sharp)^i \sigma=(F_\sharp)^j \sigma$. As a consequence, there is a ray in $(F_\sharp)^i \sigma$ that is fixed by $F^{j-i}$, so the circle map induced by $F$ has a periodic point.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise the forward orbit of a sector repeats by pigeonhole, yielding a ray fixed by an iterate, i.e. a periodic point.

nodes.name: Conclude rationality
nodes.statement: In either case, the rotation number of $F$ is rational because there is a periodic point. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Both cases produce a periodic point, so the rotation number is rational.

nodes.name: Algorithm for finding the rotation number of a piecewise linear automorphism $F$
nodes.statement: Our proof also gives an algorithm for finding the rotation number of a piecewise linear automorphism $F$. First, find a fan $\fan$ that is compatible with $F$. Then find a regular refinement $\fan'$ of $\Delta$ such that every ray in $\fan'$ is deterministic for $F_\sharp$. This can be done effectively by Lemma~\ref{lem:regularization}, Lemma~\ref{lem:regular_refinement}, and Proposition~\ref{prop:decomposition}. Tracing the orbit of each ray in $\Delta'$, as we did in the above proof, will locate the sectors containing periodic (real) rays, and this will then give the rotation number of $F$.
nodes.statement_short: Refine to a compatible regular fan with all rays deterministic, then trace ray orbits to find the periodic sectors and read off the rotation number.

nodes.name: Find a compatible fan
nodes.statement: First, find a fan $\fan$ that is compatible with $F$.
nodes.statement_short: Initialize with any fan compatible with $F$.

nodes.name: Refine to a deterministic regular fan
nodes.statement: Then find a regular refinement $\fan'$ of $\Delta$ such that every ray in $\fan'$ is deterministic for $F_\sharp$. This can be done effectively by Lemma~\ref{lem:regularization}, Lemma~\ref{lem:regular_refinement}, and Proposition~\ref{prop:decomposition}.
nodes.statement_short: Refine until regular and every ray is deterministic, effectively via Lemmas 3.1, 3.2 and Proposition 3.3.

nodes.name: Trace ray orbits and read off the rotation number
nodes.statement: Tracing the orbit of each ray in $\Delta'$, as we did in the above proof, will locate the sectors containing periodic (real) rays, and this will then give the rotation number of $F$.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate each ray to find periodic sectors, which determine the rotation number.

nodes.name: Necessity of the condition $F(\Z^2)=\Z^2$
nodes.statement: We stress here that in the definition of piecewise linear automorphism, the condition $F(\Z^2)=\Z^2$ is crucial for the Theorem A to hold. If we only require that $F(\Z^2)\subseteq\Z^2$, then it is easy to find a linear map, e.g., $F=\left[\begin{smallmatrix} 4 & -3 \\ 3 & 4 \end{smallmatrix}\right]$ such that the corresponding circle homeomorphism has an irrational rotation number.
nodes.statement_short: Weakening $F(\Z^2)=\Z^2$ to an inclusion breaks Theorem A: the matrix $\left[\begin{smallmatrix} 4 & -3 \\ 3 & 4 \end{smallmatrix}\right]$ has irrational rotation number.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem A, part II
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that for any given integer $n\ge 3$, we can find a piecewise linear automorphism $F$ of $\Z^2$ such that $\rho(F)=1/n$. For each integer $n\ge 3$ we can find a regular fan $\fan$ with $n$ sectors, say $\sigma_0,\sigma_1,\cdots,\sigma_n=\sigma_0$, arranged in the counterclockwise order. Since each $\sigma_i$ is regular, there is a unique $L_i\in \SL_2(\Z)$ such that $L_i$ maps $\sigma_i$ bijectively onto $\sigma_{i+1}$, $i=0,\cdots,n-1$ and maps the lattice points in $\sigma_i$ bijectively onto lattice points in $\sigma_{i+1}$. Define $F$ as $F|_{\sigma_i}=L_i|_{\sigma_i}$, i.e., $F$ is rotating the sectors, sending $\sigma_i$ to $\sigma_{i+1}$. Then $F$ is periodic of period $n$, and therefore $\rho(F)=1/n$.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit construction: rotate the $n$ sectors of a regular fan by the unimodular maps between consecutive sectors, giving a period-$n$ map with $\rho(F)=1/n$.

nodes.name: Reduce to $\rho(F)=1/n$
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that for any given integer $n\ge 3$, we can find a piecewise linear automorphism $F$ of $\Z^2$ such that $\rho(F)=1/n$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce realizing every rational to realizing $1/n$ for each $n\ge 3$.

nodes.name: Construct a regular fan with $n$ sectors
nodes.statement: For each integer $n\ge 3$ we can find a regular fan $\fan$ with $n$ sectors, say $\sigma_0,\sigma_1,\cdots,\sigma_n=\sigma_0$, arranged in the counterclockwise order.
nodes.statement_short: Build a regular fan whose $n$ sectors are cyclically ordered.

nodes.name: Define $F$ by rotating the sectors
nodes.statement: Since each $\sigma_i$ is regular, there is a unique $L_i\in \SL_2(\Z)$ such that $L_i$ maps $\sigma_i$ bijectively onto $\sigma_{i+1}$, $i=0,\cdots,n-1$ and maps the lattice points in $\sigma_i$ bijectively onto lattice points in $\sigma_{i+1}$. Define $F$ as $F|_{\sigma_i}=L_i|_{\sigma_i}$, i.e., $F$ is rotating the sectors, sending $\sigma_i$ to $\sigma_{i+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Glue the unique unimodular maps between consecutive regular sectors into a sector-rotating $F$.

nodes.name: Conclude $\rho(F)=1/n$
nodes.statement: Then $F$ is periodic of period $n$, and therefore $\rho(F)=1/n$.
nodes.statement_short: Periodicity of period $n$ gives rotation number $1/n$.
